label: Keeled Scales
description: Will Johnson (Centro-matic, South San Gabriel) sings in a craggy, weathered rasp over spare, atmospheric folk-rock built from acoustic guitar, brushed drums and low organ drones. It is unhurried, private-feeling songwriting, closer to a late-night confession than a rock record.
lineage: Johnson recorded a joint album with Jason Molina (Molina and Johnson, 2009), a direct link to V1; this solo record carries that haunted, Crazy Horse-shaded Americana into a quieter register.
borderline_note: Placed in V1 (named in that lane's own definition as part of the Will Johnson orbit) with C2 as secondary for its barroom-storyteller feel.

label: Keeled Scales
description: A hushed, spare set built from historical fragments, including the Spanish Civil War setting of 'Teruel', matching Johnson's plainspoken, weathered voice to sparse guitar and occasional strings. It sits at the quiet, wounded end of his catalog, for listeners who like slow, patient songs.
lineage: Continues Johnson's solo work after Centro-matic and his 2009 collaboration with Jason Molina (V1), in a quieter, more skeletal register.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Desert-toned cosmic country: reverb-heavy pedal steel, loping tempos and Shane Renfro's high, reedy voice drifting over slow-building arrangements. The songs take their time, letting guitars and steel smear into a warm, dusty haze. It suits listeners who want country rock with a psychedelic, heat-shimmer feel.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Gram Parsons-style country rock filtered through desert psychedelia, akin to 2010s cosmic-country revivalists like Promised Land Sound and twain.

label: Keeled Scales
description: A short EP of slow-motion, synth-tinged dream-folk from Carly Bond's Bay Area project: sparse arrangements, cavernous reverb and a fragile, close-mic'd vocal at the center. The songs drift rather than build, suited to late-night, headphone listening.
lineage: Extends Meernaa's hushed songwriting, which sounds suspended between Duster-style haze and modern indie folk.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Mat Davidson's twain project sets a high, keening voice against loose, fingerpicked country-folk with occasional bursts of full-band warmth. It's intimate cosmic country, closer to a campfire than a road trip.
lineage: Davidson's songwriting sounds indebted to Gram Parsons-style cosmic country and old-time singing, filtered through a DIY, small-label folk scene.

label: Keeled Scales
description: A warmer, more full-band twain record than its predecessors, still built around Davidson's reedy tenor but adding lightly psychedelic guitar textures and looser tempos. It keeps the intimacy of the earlier records while opening the windows a little, suited to slow afternoon listening.
lineage: Continues the sound of Rare Feeling with a slightly fuller studio palette, still indebted to cosmic country.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Why Bonnie's debut full-length trades their earlier bedroom dream pop for raw-edged, feedback-streaked indie rock with a Texas twang in the melodies. Blair Howerton's clear, unhurried voice rides over fuzzy guitars and road-trip imagery. It suits listeners who like their '90s-style alt-rock with a hint of country dust.
lineage: A Texas band's move from dream pop toward a more country-and-alt-rock-inflected sound, resembling the wider indie-twang turn without being a straight country record.
borderline_note: Primarily a slacker/indie-rock record; C1 given as secondary for its explicit Townes Van Zandt/Blaze Foley-referencing songwriting and Texas road-song content.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Hushed, minor-key indie folk built from finger-picked guitar and Lucille's airy, wavering voice, with lyrics circling grief, darkness and the underworld. The arrangements stay sparse and patient, leaving plenty of silence around the voice. It is for listeners who want folk that feels like a quiet room at dusk.
lineage: Sounds akin to the 2010s Bandcamp-era hushed indie folk around Keeled Scales, closer to private chamber folk than to country.

label: Keeled Scales
description: A dreamy, lo-fi debut from a Louisiana songwriter working partly in French, mixing Cajun-inflected folk melody with woozy, four-track-style production. Soft guitar and murmured vocals give it a hazy, half-remembered quality, for listeners who like quiet records with a strong sense of place.
lineage: Draws on South Louisiana's French-language song tradition, while its hushed production sounds akin to Bandcamp-era indie folk.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Piano-led songs from a longtime Phosphorescent keyboardist stepping into her own material, with slow-building, emotionally direct arrangements built around Schornikow's plainspoken alto. The pace is patient and the production uncluttered, suiting listeners who like quiet, piano-centered songwriting.
lineage: A session-musician's turn to solo songwriting, closer in spirit to the piano-based end of indie folk/slowcore than to any single scene.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Jazzy, warm-toned folk mixing loose acoustic guitar and piano with unhurried melodic turns that owe as much to Randy Newman as to any folk revivalist. Durant's relaxed, conversational singing keeps the songs intimate. It suits listeners who like their singer-songwriter records warm and a little old-fashioned.
lineage: Sounds indebted to '70s piano-and-guitar singer-songwriter craft more than to the folk revival, sitting at the jazzier edge of 2010s indie folk.

label: Tell 'Em Tapes
description: A lo-fi indie-folk EP of intimate, close-mic'd acoustic songs, with soft vocals sitting right up against fingerpicked guitar. It is bedroom-scale and diaristic, for listeners who like quiet, unvarnished songwriting.
lineage: Sounds akin to the hushed, Bandcamp-era indie folk of artists like Julia Lucille.
borderline_note: Found via the Keeled Scales catalog (a later home for the artist); this earlier EP itself was released on Tell 'Em Tapes, confirmed on its own Bandcamp page.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A compilation of Aaron Dowdy's early home-recorded songs, released as a single sprawling document of the years before Fust became a full band. Rough, home-taped country songs with Dowdy's drawl up front show the roots of the band's later, fuller storytelling. It is for fans who want to hear the sketches behind the band records.
lineage: Predates and directly seeds the full-band Fust sound heard on Genevieve and Big Ugly; a look at the songwriter's home-recording origins before the Dear Life Records band era.
borderline_note: A compilation of early home-recorded EPs rather than a single planned album; included as a documented prequel to Fust's later, already-staged LPs.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A shifting North Carolina collective recording traditional ballads and hymns with tape manipulation and found-sound production. String-band playing drifts in and out of hiss, drones and field-recording textures, so the inherited songs feel half-remembered. It is for listeners who want folk tradition treated as raw material for experiment.
lineage: Sounds rooted in the Piedmont old-time/string-band tradition, while its Dear Life Records home ties it to the same DIY label network as Sluice and Fust.
borderline_note: Closer to experimental old-time/noise than to the twang-rock core of C5; kept here for its Dear Life/Sluice ties, with V8 (American Primitive/drone folk) as secondary.

label: Dear Life Records
description: Michael Cormier-O'Leary's chamber-folk project Hour opens up into a larger ensemble of winds, strings and mallet percussion for slow, meditative pieces. It sits closer to instrumental chamber music than a rock record, patient and quietly mournful. For listeners who like slowcore's pacing without the guitars.
lineage: Cormier-O'Leary also plays in Friendship, and Hour shares Dear Life Records with that Philadelphia deadpan/slowcore circle.
borderline_note: Mostly instrumental chamber-folk rather than twang; included under C8's hushed/sparse definition for its Dear Life/Cormier-O'Leary lineage.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A live album gathered from Hour's DIY touring, capturing the shifting chamber-folk ensemble in intimate, informal rooms. Winds, strings and quiet percussion breathe around slow, meditative pieces, with the audience close enough to hear. It is a touring-diary counterpart to the studio records.
lineage: A touring-diary document in Hour's catalog before Ghost Bridge, part of the same Dear Life Records world as Cormier-O'Leary's band Friendship.

label: Lame-O Records
description: Dave Benton's Trace Mountains project leans further into warmly recorded, country-tinged indie pop on this record, mixing jangling guitars with synths and unhurried melodies. Benton's soft, conversational voice keeps things intimate even when the arrangements fill out. It suits listeners who like gentle, twang-flecked indie rock.
lineage: A former LVL UP member's move toward twangier songwriting, released on Philadelphia's Lame-O Records alongside Slaughter Beach, Dog; its country tint sounds akin to the wider indie-twang turn.

label: Lame-O Records
description: Matt Scottoline's Hurry plays tight, hook-forward power pop with an easy, unfussy jangle and plainspoken lyrics about heartbreak and self-doubt. The songs are short, sunny-sounding and quietly anxious underneath. It is for listeners who like their guitar pop clean and catchy.
lineage: Part of Philadelphia's Lame-O Records power-pop circle; the sound is indebted to Big Star and Superchunk.

label: Lame-O Records
description: A sprawling double set of concise, hook-driven power pop split into 'Girls' and 'Boys' halves, led by Peter Gill, who also plays in Friendship. The songs are quick, bright and jangly, flying past before they can outstay their welcome. It suits listeners who like power pop in big, generous doses.
lineage: Gill's membership in Friendship ties 2nd Grade to the same Philadelphia scene as Friendship and Hurry; the songwriting sounds indebted to Big Star and Guided by Voices.

label: Lame-O Records
description: A brief burst of ringing, mid-fi guitar pop from another corner of Lame-O's Philadelphia power-pop stable, all hooks and no filler. Bright, chiming guitars and easy melodies keep it light on its feet. It is a quick hit for fans of short, sweet jangle.
lineage: Sounds akin to the Philadelphia jangle-pop of Hurry and 2nd Grade.

label: Alive Naturalsound Records
description: A laid-back homage to '70s Topanga Canyon and Marin County sounds from a band built around former Beachwood Sparks members: jangly, country-tinged FM rock full of easy harmonies. Warm guitars and unhurried tempos make it sound like a lost mid-'70s radio record. It suits listeners who like breezy, sun-bleached country rock.
lineage: Formed by Beachwood Sparks' Brent Rademaker, directly continuing that band's cosmic-country line.

label: Curation
description: The 2000s cosmic-country revivalists' first album in over a decade, mixing pedal-steel-laced country rock with the band's longtime dreamy, harmony-driven sound. The songs drift at easy tempos with jangling guitars and soft group vocals. It is a warm late-career return for fans of their early records.
lineage: A late-career return from one of the foundational 2000s cosmic-country revival bands (C6); their sound is indebted to V21 country rock and the Paisley Underground's jangle.
borderline_note: Band's classic-era catalog (2000-2012) is V-zone Paisley Underground territory; this 2024 record alone is Core-era and staged here.

label: Paradise of Bachelors
description: A young Nashville band's second album, expanding from garage-country burners into ambitious, Byrds- and Big Star-indebted psych-country. Twin guitars, ringing harmonies and long instrumental stretches give it a loose, '70s feel. It suits listeners who like cosmic country with a bit of rock-and-roll grit.
lineage: Released by Paradise of Bachelors, tying it to that label's American-vernacular roster; the sound is indebted to the Byrds and Big Star.

label: Paradise of Bachelors
description: Erin Birgy's surrealist song-world turns painterly and desert-lit on this record, co-produced with Big Thief's James Krivchenia. Avant-pop arrangements of horns, synths and loose guitar wrap around plainspoken, image-dense lyrics. It suits listeners who like their indie folk strange and colorful.
lineage: Connected to the Big Thief/indie-folk network via Krivchenia's production; sits at the arty edge of the twangy indie-folk lane.
borderline_note: More art-pop than twang; included as a borderline C5 fit given its acoustic-folk backbone and Big Thief-circle production ties.

label: Paradise of Bachelors
description: A slightly more polished, full-band record that keeps Nigel Chapman's signature talk-singing but adds more melodic hooks and confident guitar solos. It is the band's most accessible entry point, warm and ringing without losing its bookish, self-questioning lyrics.
lineage: Explicitly indebted to Pavement, the Clean, the Go-Betweens and Silver Jews-style deadpan songwriting, making Nap Eyes a direct continuation of the C7 slacker/jangle lineage.

label: Orindal Records
description: Owen Ashworth's post-Casiotone project sets deadpan, plainly sung short stories about Michigan, Christmas and lost people over minimal drum machine and synth. The songs are small and exact, with the quiet electronics leaving the narratives in front.
lineage: Carries the deadpan storytelling of the Drag City school (Silver Jews) into Ashworth's own Orindal Records orbit, following directly from his Casiotone for the Painfully Alone records.

label: Orindal Records
description: Friendship frontman Dan Wriggins' solo debut EP: minimal, open-frame production (organ, quiet drums, classical guitar) behind fragmentary, prose-poem lyrics delivered in a solemn, wounded voice.
lineage: Wriggins cites Kath Bloom and Vic Chesnutt as models; a direct extension of his alt-country band Friendship's deadpan storytelling into a solo, more skeletal form.

label: Orindal Records
description: The Ohmme co-founder's solo debut: spare piano- and violin-inflected songs moving between chamber-folk intimacy and quiet dissonance. Her clear voice sits close to the listener while strings scrape and hover at the edges. It suits listeners who like experimental folk that stays tender.
lineage: Grows out of Chicago's overlapping indie-folk/experimental scene, tied to Orindal labelmates Gia Margaret and Macie Stewart's other Chicago projects.

label: Dalliance Recordings
description: A hushed, lo-fi debut of whispery vocals over sparse acoustic guitar and piano, later reissued via the Orindal Records-adjacent Chicago scene.
lineage: Sits alongside Chicago's Orindal/Dear Nora/Advance Base circle of quiet, home-recorded songwriting.
borderline_note: Original label is Dalliance Recordings, not Orindal; discovered via the Orindal catalog page, year/label confirmed on the artist's own Bandcamp page.

label: Keeled Scales / Orindal Records
description: A Tucson artist's record blending Americana-tinged songwriting with ambient sound design: synthesizer, tape loops, field recordings and desert-referencing lyrics. Songs dissolve into long drones and hiss before re-forming around her voice and guitar. It is for listeners who like folk that shades into ambient music.
lineage: A joint release between Keeled Scales and Orindal Records, connecting Tucson's desert-folk scene to both labels' networks.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Durant's newer record continues her warm, jazz-inflected folk songwriting, now on Ruination Record Co. Loose guitar, piano and relaxed, conversational vocals keep the songs intimate and unhurried. It suits listeners who liked the easy, old-fashioned warmth of Islands.
lineage: A continuation of the jazz-tinged folk songwriting heard on her earlier Keeled Scales record Islands.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Dan Knishkowy's Adeline Hotel project offers gentle, fingerpicked indie folk with plainspoken, slightly wry lyrics about memory and routine. Soft vocals and small arrangements keep it homey and understated. It suits listeners who like quiet, detail-focused songwriting.
lineage: Sounds akin to a small Brooklyn songwriter circle around Ruination Record Co.; fingerpicked folk with a deadpan streak.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: A piano-led, songs-first country record from the Fust bassist and Dear Life Records co-owner, mixing Neil Young-style keyboard balladry with Lambchop-esque narrative turns and field-recording interludes.
lineage: Meadows co-runs Dear Life Records and plays in Fust, linking this solo record directly to that North Carolina/Brooklyn alt-country network.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: A Brooklyn songwriter's guitar-and-synth indie rock record, made with players from the Ruination Record Co. circle. Clean guitars and glowing synths frame understated vocals and mid-tempo songs. It suits listeners who like thoughtful, low-key indie rock.
lineage: Part of the same small Brooklyn songwriter-collaborator scene as Adeline Hotel, Office Culture and The Bird Calls.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Sam Sodomsky's songwriting project sounds akin to David Berman, John Darnielle and Dan Bejar: clever, plainspoken songs balancing folksy earnestness against wry self-awareness. Gentle guitar arrangements leave room for the lyrics to do the work. It suits listeners who come to songs for the words.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the deadpan-songwriter lineage of Berman and Darnielle, within the small Brooklyn Ruination Record Co. circle.
key_tracks: To Everything There Is A Ceiling

label: Polyvinyl
description: Ella Williams's fourth Squirrel Flower album is dense, expansive guitar rock about work, anxiety and climate dread, cut with Alex Farrar (MJ Lenderman, Wednesday) and players from Wednesday, Bon Iver and the War on Drugs.
lineage: Farrar's production ties Squirrel Flower directly into the Asheville Drop of Sun network that also produced Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.
borderline_note: Straighter indie rock than most of C1, but included for its direct Alex Farrar/Wednesday-circle production credits.

album: Say a Prayer to the Gods of Getting Going
label: Polyvinyl
description: Ella Williams' enveloping voice sits against crunchy, wall-of-guitar production on this Squirrel Flower record. Big, distorted guitars swell under slow, open melodies, giving the songs a live, room-filling weight. It suits listeners who like loud guitars wrapped around intimate songwriting.
lineage: Continues Squirrel Flower's move toward the countrygaze-adjacent, guitar-wall sound of Wednesday's circle.
